utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. And may we hear the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Ann Sutherland with Ruth Karper for the Def -- Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. For the real Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. John Ostojic and our case manager, Danilo Cirkovic, on behalf of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then any issues to be discussed before we start?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple issues I'd like to raise with the Court. I'd like to do it, though, after this witness just so we could perhaps conclude him. They don't involve this witness, but there are two separate issues that I'd like to raise when it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed this way. Prosecution, any issues to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are prepared to continue with the examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The floor is yours, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, Mr. Rosic. My name is John Ostojic along with Danilo Cirkovic; we represent Dr. Stakic. Once again, thank you for your patience. I only have a couple of areas that I hope to cover with you this afternoon, and then the representation and the Office of the Prosecution will conduct their examination, as will the Honourable Court. I'd like to clarify two points. One involves the travel that you conducted from Omarska to the city/town of Prijedor. Can you share with us if during those travels, you encountered or saw any barricades or checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, barricades along the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road appeared as early as April. I saw them in April, not on the road itself but by the side of the road. However, as early as May, barricades were set up along the road itself. Those were old trailers for trucks, and then there were obstacles made of iron.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the road that leads -- or the road of Banja Luka/Prijedor that leads into Prijedor, can you just name or identify several towns or villages that appear along that road.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Omarska, there is Lamovita, Kamicani, Kozarac, Kozarusa, Orlovaca, and Prijedor, which means that when you set out from Omarska in the direction of Prijedor, at 6 kilometres, you come across Kamicani, which is a predominantly Muslim village. Then there are Kozarac and Kozarusa. And then on to as far as 3 kilometres just outside Prijedor, those are predominantly Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And share with us, if you would, whether or not the checkpoints and barricades that you observed were within the towns which were populated predominantly by Muslims; namely, I'm interested in Kozarac and Kozarusa. Do you recall, sir, seeing the barricades while in those towns specifically prior to April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. In Kozarusa, if you come in from the direction of Prijedor, in the village of Kozarusa itself, that's on the road at a junction where the road forks off in the direction of Kozarac. There was -- in the direction of Kozarusa, there was a barricade next to the road itself. I wasn't -- I was passing every day, and I saw other things that were even more unusual. People were preparing to block the road. The same thing in the village, when you go from Omarska in Kozarac at the junction, there was a container that had been put there, a metal container used mostly in offices. But there was something there that hadn't been there up to that point, and in Kamicani, too, I noticed, that's about 6 kilometres from Omarska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, do you know the individuals who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, do you know whether or not the individuals who were at these checkpoints and barricades in Kamicani, Kozarac, and Kozarusa, whether they were armed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that they were armed, yes. By coincidence, it was exactly at the checkpoint in Kozarusa, a colleague, a driver who worked for communal services was one of the people manning the checkpoint in Kozarusa. I knew this person. I knew him personally. Of course, they were armed. He was carrying a hunting rifle, a double-barrel hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you, sir, tell us the name of this individual, or would you rather that we go into private session to identify him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I'm permitted to invite the witness to make that decision, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mind. I can also proceed in open session. Sead Causevic, that's his name. His father's name is Saban. I know this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this individual, Mr. Causevic, he worked with you in the Department of Communal Services. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was a driver for communal services. And before the war, he had -- he was in charge of special tasks. He was in charge of catching and killing stray dogs and cats around the town of Prijedor. That was his service. Even back then, he had a weapon and a license for that weapon issued by communal services. Communal services would issue a weapon to people who were in charge of these tasks I have described. As early as the beginning of April, he stopped coming to work, and he never returned the weapon that he had signed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you for that. And that is my follow-up question. As an employee of the Department of Communal Services, was Mr. Causevic terminated, dismissed from his employment, or did he voluntarily resign?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left of his own free will. I think in early April, and he never returned to the company where he used to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, do you know why he resigned voluntarily as an employee from the Department of Communal Services?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could tell you why exactly, but he was a member of the SDA. And even during the pre-election campaign, he was working with the SDS [as interpreted]. So I really don't know the exact reason why he voluntarily resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, for Your Honours, on page 5, line 16, I think the witness said SDA. It appears that way immediately above that. But the translator apparently heard SDS, that he was working with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the best way to correct this is to ask the same question a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, I will. If you don't mind, Your Honour, can I just clarify that issue with him in the manner which I think is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, just to clarify a point because we're having some trouble with the translation, it states here that you mentioned that: "And even during the pre-election campaign, he - and I'm inserting I think you're talking about Mr. Causevic - was working with the SDS." Was Mr. Causevic working with the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He was working for the SDA, not the SDS. SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. I'd like to turn to a different issue, if I may, sir. In late 1992, are you familiar with any action that was commenced relating to Dr. Stakic and removing him as being president of the Municipal Assembly of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about that, but I can't remember the exact date. I can't remember the exact date. Maybe it was in late 1992. However, word was around Prijedor that deputy Srdjo Srdic was saying that Stakic was not fit for his job, that he could no longer keep the same position. So the secretary of the SDS, Simo Miskovic, was negotiating with Srdjo Srdic to remove Dr. Stakic from his position. And he was removed, but I can't remember exactly whether it was still in 1992 or 1993. However, I know it for a fact they were talking about Dr. Stakic not being fit to keep that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions we have at this time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution, proceed with the cross-examination. Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, a moment ago you said that prior to the 30th of April, 1992, you saw barricades and checkpoints by the side of the road of Muslim villages between Omarska and Prijedor. And you said that the persons at these checkpoints were armed. They were mixed checkpoints, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were mixed or not. I can't claim what the exact nature of those checkpoints was. I know that there were checkpoints there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There were also checkpoints in Serb villages, for example, Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Orlovci, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to some topics that you gave evidence about yesterday. Are you aware of the exact legal relationship between the Municipal Assembly and its executive council?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, I believe, are people who have been elected, deputies. And the executive body of government is the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. The Executive Board which then has a number of ministries and work units depending on the area of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're not aware of the exact legal relationship in relation to delegated authority and power, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not able to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is it true that housing is linked to employment? So, for example, if - and I'm moving now to another topic - if you're employed by a company, and you lose your employment, isn't it also true that you would lose your housing?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question -- pardon me. If I can object to the form of the question, Your Honour. I'm not sure if she is talking in what time frame, and I'd hate to speculate. And she could just preface for us if it's current, before 1992, during the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, or during the period within the parametres of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'll take it in two stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, under SFRY law, if you lost your employment, you would also then lose your house, would you not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If your housing was linked to your job, if your housing was provided by your employer, is it not correct that if you lost your job, you would also then lose your house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The housing would be completely unrelated if you lost your job. It didn't necessarily mean you would lose your flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Even if it was provided by your employer whom you no longer worked for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, same thing. He may have fired me, my employer, but he couldn't take my flat from me. So I was still free to use and entitled to use the flat. No one could take your flat, your house, away from you. Having been fired made no difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I think I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should have a chance to rethink his answer. Maybe the answer is not plausible, and maybe you even have misunderstood the question. Given the case your employer is the owner of the house you're living in and then you're fired, wouldn't be at the same time that you would have to leave this house or this flat owned by your employer as a fired employee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understood the question fully. If I, for example, worked for a certain company and the company fired me, I left this company and I went to a different company and found a job in this other company, but I kept my right to stay in the same flat that I had been in before. No one could take that right away from me. That was all according to regulations of the former Yugoslavia. I was allowed and entitled even to keep my flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, you, in 1992, were not a member of the SDS, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I wasn't. I wasn't, no. I wasn't that in 1992 or before 1992 or after it, nor am I today. I still do not belong to any party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In 1990, were you a member of the reformist party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reformist, no. No, I was never a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that Dr. Stakic had a brother. What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People call him Baco. But his name is -- I wouldn't really know because we all call him Baco, Baco Stakic. Everybody refers to him that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he work at the iron ore mine? No, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sure. No, he did not work there, I'm sure. He worked in Rijeka as far as I know and came back sometime in 1991. I'm not sure about that. What I do know, however, is that he did not work in the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you're not aware that his brother was called Milorad Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. We all call him Baco. This is his pet name, his nickname. And that is how I know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene once again. As a member of the family, please concentrate on the question. The question clearly was the name of the brother of Dr. Stakic, Milorad Stakic, yes or no? Because there is a strong likelihood that you, in fact, know the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could be Milomir or Milorad. I mean, I can't remember perhaps because we all called him Baco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sir, this is not a guessing game. You are under a solemn declaration. And please don't try to tell us that the brother has the same name as Dr. Milomir Stakic. I'm quite sure you know the name of the brother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never said they had the same name. Milomir and Milorad are two different ones. But whether he's Milorad, I cannot really say positively, and that is why I said only Baco. But that is not his name; that is his nickname. That is people call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sir, a final attempt, and please be aware that you're under solemn declaration: What is the name of the brother of Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you. I can't say positively something that I do not know. I know they call him Baco. If you show me his photograph, I'll tell you yes, that's he. But otherwise anything that I might say would be -- would be incorrect. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, when were you first asked to testify in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as a distant relative of Dr. Stakic, you're not happy to find him on trial, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm not happy. Quite naturally, I can't be happy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you testified yesterday that after the 30th of May, 1992, your work unit had to clean up the area of Prijedor after the attack. It was predominantly Muslim houses that had been destroyed and burnt and looted during this attack, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To that area where the Muslim houses were, we never went there. We were cleaning up parts of the town between buildings, structures, major ones. But we never went into localities. It was our priority to clean up the centre of the town. And we also did it manually because we had no mechanical devices. All we had was a truck that we loaded things on to. Otherwise, we didn't have anything. And all this was rubbish, glass, shattered glass shards and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of buildings were you cleaning up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not clean up buildings. Next to the buildings, the centre around buildings, next to the buildings, the pavements, parks, streets. But we did not go into those localities where private small houses predominate. We did not go to those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see damage to Muslim settlements in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes. I did see that, but I didn't go in. What one could see with the naked eye, I saw that there were houses destroyed and...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you also see the destruction of Stari Grad settlement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but from a distance of about 50 to 100 metres because there is a brook there I didn't cross over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness out of the bundle, Madam Registrar, please help me, the exhibit number, S235-9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please explain what document this is you can find on the ELMO right now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jahorina insurance policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see "Mil."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You need not look on the --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stakic, Stakic. Milorad. Milorad, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it's easier for you, you may look on the document on your right-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Stakic, Milorad. Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the name -- and the place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 8th of January, 1958, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So who would be this person? Would it be a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be. Born in 1958. Could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know the age of the brother of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We couldn't hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's younger than Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could it be that he's born actually in 1958?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's younger than that. 1960-something rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Where does the brother live in the moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now he lives in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please, what is the address?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the name of the street, but he's in Prijedor, and it's a building behind the electric facility. I don't know exactly what the street is called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please, once again, have a look on this document, you can see an address as well. Could you please read this address aloud.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Prijedor, Raskovica 53, I think, or is it 20 -- but it's Raskovica. The street is Raskavica. No, he's not in that street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know another member of the family of Dr. Stakic with the name of Milorad Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one Mico Stakic. He's a relative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think my question was clear enough. Is there another member of the family of Dr. Stakic with the name of Milorad Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, in his family, his brother and he, they are first -- brothers of the first blood. But there are also other related Stakics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to ask the same question for the third time: Is there any other member of the family of Dr. Stakic with the name of Milorad Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- the members of the family are he and his brother. But he has relatives who share the surname Stakic but who are more removed relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just ask the interpreter just to review the videotape because I think the witness answered slightly differently and said in the beginning of his comment "ne postoji." And I think he answered the Court's question even prior to that. So I would just ask them to look at that issue or just mark it in the record and we could view it at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this case, the formal procedure would be a written request for review of the video. Having seen now this document, the address, the name of -- the date of birth, did you ever discuss the fate of Dr. Stakic with his brother as a member of the family, that he's arrested here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I never talked with him about -- that is, we don't see each other often, and it is usually in passing, so that I was never with him to talk about the fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever try to call him by telephone to know what's happening with this person you were acquainted with, person who is a member of your family, your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I didn't by telephone or -- by telephone or -- I don't even know his number. And we only communicate with the father, father Milan and mother Mira. And since he's in Prijedor, I'm in Omarska, so when I go to work or come back, I sometimes meet him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you to speak up or more loudly, please, because it's extremely difficult for the interpreters and also for us to follow you. And could you please repeat the end of your last sentence on the question whether you ever contacted him by telephone or --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not communicate with him, with Milomir's brother, never. I don't know his number. And on a couple of occasions, I saw him in passing so that I did not communicate with him or rather discuss with him his brother's fate. But I did go to his father Milan, and we talked about it. "What do you think about it?" "Well, I think" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again, we could not hear the end of the witness's sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing special to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I once again ask you to speak up that we and the interpreters can hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can the usher also please move the microphones forward a little, please, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown S235-71, S235-70.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you identify the name and can you identify what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well. The first part, the name is Milorad Stakic, Milorad. Milo -- this is like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can understand it's difficult --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stakic, Milovan, maybe. Stakic. Profession -- this is unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order to save time, can you tell us what was the car that was driven by or owned by the brother of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you what the car was because I don't know what car he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You know his nickname. You have met you stated --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baco. Baco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, you know his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you tell us you don't know the car this person owned.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown first the other document.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MP Autotransport Prijedor, Stakic Milorad, 15 December 2000. The type of goods, tech, quantity 12, price nothing, total nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently these documents do not fresh up your recollection one step further. Document S235-81. Can you identify what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a traffic license for a vehicle. It's a traffic license -- a traffic license for a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who is the owner of the car?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Stakic. The identity number 2509965160008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the address?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The address, Jovana Raskovica, no number, Republika Srpska, Prijedor. The date of issuance, 14 December, and this is 19 -- is it a 9? I can't see too well. It's 1998, maybe, or maybe 19 -- 10603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data on the first registration, the 14th of December, 1998. Prijedor. Registration plates number 412-K-087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please continue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Passenger. Volkswagen. VW Golf. L/3. Metallic green, light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Does this ring a bell? Have you ever seen the brother of Dr. Stakic with a Volkswagen Golf in this colour?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever having seen him in a green Golf. I can see here that this is a Golf because all the information is about the Golf car. But I don't have any such recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said: "I don't remember ever having seen him in a green Golf." What car did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him in a car. I saw him in passing, but I don't know what car he drove, what car he had come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So then I may finally ask you to first have a look, and then please to read out at least in part, Document S235-14 and 15. By the way, do you know the date of birth of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The age?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was born in 1964, as far as I can remember. But I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please first tell us what kind of document this is we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please lower down the ELMO so I can see better. This is a decision, Milan, Milomir Stakic from Prijedor. "Mira Milana Tepica Street Number 19, January 1962 in Prijedor. Profession: Physician. Married, two children. A citizen of Republika Srpska with a university degree, high qualification. Monthly salary: 600 German marks." According to his own statement so far without any convictions nor is he under any investigation. He is responsible and accounts for importing into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia against the provisions of the law on foreign trade Article 88 and Article 89. He imported a passenger vehicle Golf registration plates 412-K-087, the year of production, 1981. The number of chassis, WVWZZZI7Z8W258967. The number of engine, GG158224, which has been registered in the name of Milorad Stakic. And he drove the car -- the same car in Belgrade on the 6th of September 2000. By doing that, he committed a violation pursuant to Article 99, paragraph 1, item 1 of the law on traffic misdemeanours. For that, the commission for customs violations of the customs office in Belgrade finds him guilty and punishes him -- and orders him to pay a fine of 3.000 dinars. Shall I continue reading? "The above -- the aforementioned fine shall be paid within 15 days from the day when this decision comes into force. The fine will be paid into the account of the customs office in Belgrade, number 40818-697-5-2619. If the fine is not paid within the deadline and if the money cannot be collected, then the person will be sentenced to a prison sentence and a special decision will be issued on that. Paragraph 2: "The goods which are the subject of this misdemeanour, in this case, it is a passenger vehicle, Golf, registration plates 412-K-087, previously described in paragraph 1 of this decision, shall not be seized pursuant to Article 100 of the law on traffic misdemeanours. The vehicle will be returned to the owner, Milorad Stakic, in terms of the authorities pursuant to Article 91 of the law on -- the law on -- the vehicle is currently -- has been put under the supervision of the customs office Belgrade under D11162000 dated 12 of September, 2002. Paragraph 3: "The accused is bound pursuant to Article 99 of the law of misdemeanours and 26A of the law on compensation of damages in misdemeanours proceedings conducted by the federal bodies, Official Gazette 12/2000, to pay 200 dinars on behalf of the expenses incurred by the proceedings into the giro account of the customs office in Belgrade number 40818-697-5-2619. "Minutes taken by: Members of the commission deputy of the president commission, Mirjana Ostasevic-Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is enough from this document. May I ask you once again, do you know the aforementioned Milorad Stakic, apparently any close relationship to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly because I don't know whether his brother's name is Milorad. I know that he is Baco. And as for the vehicle, I can see what it is, but I can't tell you who this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was your telephone number in your office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your private home?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before. In the meantime, the numbers have been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only for the parties, I'm making reference to document S235-48. A final area: Were you ever involved in the decision on the demolition of structures war damaged beyond repair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you in your capacity of being involved in the decision whether or not a gravel pit should be used as a temporary rubbish dump? I'm just trying to find out what is the area of your work, because until now I didn't have a clear picture what, in fact, was your duty.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duties consisted of the following: To collect garbage, we used vehicles and manpower for that. We also did sanitation. We mowed lawns in parks. We planted flowers. So we did gardening in parks. That was within my scope of work. And I received my orders from my director. He gave me my tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, the question: When a gravel pit should be used as a temporary rubbish dump, would this be in part your work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this wouldn't be part of my work. We did not deposit rubbish in gravel pit because we had a very good waste disposal site, one of the best in the region. It was forbidden to deposit garbage in the gravel pit because the drinking water comes from the area of those gravel pits. If I was to make decisions, I wouldn't allow that. But I wasn't the one to decide where rubbish would be deposited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Document S180, item number 37, page number 45. Would you please read out this document from the Official Gazette issued 2/92.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here this is in English, I believe. It says Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the B/C/S one, and the English...

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to read everything under 37?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At its meeting of 9 June, 1992, Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff pursuant to Article 7 of the decision on the organisation and work of Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff adopted the following decision: "Article 1: The unreclaimed gravel pit in the village of Miljakovci which was not been stabilised and which is denoted as KC number 79 shall be used as a temporary rubbish dump. "Article 2: The communal services will look after the implementation of this decision. "Article 3: This decision shall enter into force on the day it is adopted. "Number 02-111-162/92. Prijedor. Date: 9 June 1992. "President of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document printed out in any Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I didn't read the Official Gazette, and it is the first time I see a document like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So apparently, there seems at least to be an overlap of the work of Dr. Milomir Stakic and your own work. Did you ever discuss these questions with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with Dr. Stakic what it was his work as president of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never talked about that, nor did I deem it necessary to talk about that. I didn't even ask him whether he was president or not. I heard there was a Crisis Staff, but I never went into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's leave it with that. But I feel under the obligation to give you a last chance by putting to you once again the question after this attempt to refresh your recollection: Was the name of the brother or is the name of the brother of Dr. Stakic, Milorad Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I know that he is Baco. I'm really sorry, but I can't say something that I don't know. I can call my wife, and I can ask her what his name is, whether it is Milorad or something else. But I myself really cannot remember. Because we never called him by his first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which was the first name or the name you called Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Doctor," "Dr. Stakic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Judge Vassylenko, any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was your reaction on the election of Dr. Stakic vice-president of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, so to speak, happy that such a young man had been elected vice-president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: Did Dr. Stakic continue to live in the same apartment he lived before the election?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please specify the time period you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Just after the election as the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And I understand you were neighbours, your family and the family of Dr. Stakic lived, as you said, door-to-door and shared one yard. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that was the first house next to my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday, it's transcript page 91, that on 30th of April, "like every morning, I got up. I got into my car. I turned the engine on. And I waited for him to join me on the ride to Prijedor. He was always a few minutes late, and I decided to go and go and ring his bell. His wife, Bozana, answered the door and told me that Miso left with the police some 20 minutes ago." Had you heard the police car approaching the apartments where you lived? Have you heard some noise, voices inviting Dr. Stakic to join police and to follow them to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't hear anything. I didn't hear anything. When I came out of the house, I expected Dr. Stakic, but as I told you before, that means I did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And before, how often police pick up Dr. Stakic and transported him to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the police came on several occasions to pick him up or not. But I no longer drove him. He had his own official driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But before the takeover, you testified that each morning, you drove Dr. Stakic to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Were there occasions when police came to pick up Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the police never came to pick him up -- at least to the best of my knowledge the police didn't come. I drove him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the wife of Dr. Stakic, Bozana, that police took him to Prijedor, not yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a reaction. She said Miso had been picked up, but don't be afraid. And I didn't stay there for long because I was supposed to be on my way to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was she surprised? Upset? Angered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was quite upset. She was not indifferent, of course. Why the police? That sort of thing. But I only asked her: "So, where's Doctor?" And she said he had been picked up by the police, so that was the whole conversation between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But yesterday you testified that "I asked her what had happened, and she said `nothing really.'"

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked her why the police had picked him up, what was happening. And she said: "Well, nothing really," but I could tell that she was confused. But I went away then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And you didn't ask her what was going on, what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask. I didn't know. She only said that he had been picked up by the police, and I said: "What for?" And she said: "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 10 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to bring the witness into the courtroom. And when the usher has arrived again, may these copies of the revised scheduling order as from today may be distributed. They will be filed at the same time. Judge Vassylenko, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: My next question: Have you seen Dr. Stakic in the evening on 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see him. We were together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Now I would like to move to another area. You testified that Dr. Stakic was a member of the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And can you explain who was the founder of the People's Radical party Veljko Guberina or Nikola Pasic? Why such difference?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to explain this. I believe Nikola Pasic was only the name of the party, but I don't think any of the members were founding members. Neither Nikola nor Guberina as far as I know were alive at the time when the party was founded. Now, as to who the founder of the party was, I only know that Dr. Stakic was on their electoral list in Omarska, on the list of that party, people's radical party. He was on their list. And as the highest ranking candidate, he garnered the most votes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And then Dr. Stakic became the member of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the date. It must have been in 1990 before the elections, because he was a candidate on their list in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the position of Dr. Stakic within the people's radical party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Omarska where he was working as a general practitioner, a physician, he was a man who was held in high regard, and he was a scientist, well-respected by all the people of Omarska, and he served as an example to other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Was he an ordinary member of this party, or he was among the leadership of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the leadership of that party, in the leadership of his party, people's radical party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: He was president of the party in Omarska area or the president of the party in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president for the Omarska area, but I don't know about the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what was the platform of this party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't a member, so I couldn't tell. I don't know any of the platforms of any of the different parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And can you explain me how it happened that being a member of people's radical party Dr. Stakic became the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly as SDS representative?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to answer this question. I only know that he was in the party. Now, when he went to the SDS and became their member exactly, I don't know. But I know that before the elections in 1990, he was the president of the people's radical party for the Omarska area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. Did you have a radio in your car?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Could you listen to Radio Prijedor in your car radio?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could. I could listen to it, the local radio station, Prijedor Radio, and all the other local stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And did you usually listen to that radio?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most frequently not. I preferred to play a tape, my own tape when I travelled. So I listened to music.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And the 30th of April, knowing that your friend, relative, and neighbour had been taken to Prijedor by the police, didn't you turn on your radio to know what was happening on that precise morning?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't turn on anything. I was wondering what had happened and why that had happened, but I didn't listen to anything on the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You weren't curious about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was curious, yes. But it simply didn't occur to me to try to find out on the radio what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And when you arrived at your work, did you ask any questions? Did you try to learn what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived, when I came to work, then I was told that the army and the police had taken over the Municipal Assembly and the MUP. That's what I found out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And about your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please answer that it's reflected on the transcript and not only by gestures.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get the interpretation. I couldn't hear the interpretation. That's why I made a gesture with my hands. But yes, now I have managed to hear the question. What my reaction was, I asked what it was about, but no one was able to explain. They only said that the army and the police had taken over the Municipal Assembly and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But you knew that the police had taken your neighbour to Prijedor, and you never heard the news what was this all about related to your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that particular moment at work, among my colleagues, no one was able to explain. It was only later that I heard that the Municipal Assembly had been taken over as well as the SUP. But later on, over the following days, I heard that Stakic had been appointed the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Didn't you hear an announcement on Radio Prijedor that very morning telling the citizens of Prijedor about the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything on the radio at that time because I was at work. But others told me that there had been one, just that I wasn't listening to the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: What was your assignment, if you can remember, of work on the morning of the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assignment was as usual; however, on that day, no one was really leaving the perimeter of the company to go to work. Everyone was talking about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: That's what I supposed. Thank you. I'm turning to another subject. This morning at page 4, line 9, you were talking about barricades, and you told us that had you saw armed men. Your words were: "They were armed?" "Yes." And you told us that you found an acquaintance from school or something like that, and he was carrying a hunting rifle. Isn't it true that all the people at the barricade were carrying these sort of rifles?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all the people. Not all of them. He caught my eye because he worked in my company. I didn't see that any of the others had rifles. He had taken this rifle from the company, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the others were armed with other kind of weapons or that the others didn't carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had other types of weapons, not that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Can you please kindly tell me what kind of weapons the others had.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that checkpoint, they had a pistol. I saw it at a belt, but I can't say of which make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Every one of the persons at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were four of them at that checkpoint in a group. And he was the only one who had a rifle, and a hunting one at that, not an army rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You asked my last question. So I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just let me return to Judge Vassylenko's question on page 27, line 21. The question was: "Have you seen Dr. Stakic in the evening on 29th of April, 1992?" Isn't it true that following your testimony you all the days in the morning brought Dr. Stakic to Prijedor and in the evening back to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Every morning, I'd take him -- I'd give him a lift. But I didn't always give him a lift back home, and I've already said that. It depended on work. At times, we came back together, but not always. But on the 29th in the evening, we were together -- I mean, we were together in the evening, but I had not come together with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I fully understand that you remember very well what happened on the day of the takeover of Prijedor. But how is it possible that you can answer the question put to you by Judge Vassylenko related to the 29th of April in this clarity: "Yes, I did see him. We were together."

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? Because we were together. We were together all the time until that 30th, until that fateful day when -- we were there every day, every evening, whenever we were off duty practically. Whenever we didn't work, we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When was, in fact, the first day after the takeover you met Dr. Stakic again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. In those early days, I did not see him again. I saw him only -- I saw him again only some time in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Dr. Stakic never again came back to his home in the neighbouring house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see him come back. I asked Bozana, and she says: "He's on duty. He'll be back." But then they moved house to Prijedor in the latter half of May so that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think on the transcript, your sentence doesn't end. It reads: "But then they moved house to Prijedor in the latter half of May so that..."

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that I did not come across him in Omarska because he was not living there in the neighbourhood next door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, you answered: "No, I did not see him come back." Let me repeat, when for the first time did you meet Dr. Stakic after the takeover again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the Municipal Assembly hall because I went there to get my work orders, to the secretariat for public utilities, and then I ran across him in the passageway. But that was sometime around the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Approximately when was this? One or two days after the takeover? A month later?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, 20 days after the takeover. On the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what did you discuss with the person you were acquainted with, you had met in the past all the day --

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him: "What's this? What's going on?" And he said: "Well, you see how things are." And then I simply asked him about my nephew, my brother's son, and he said let's not talk about that. It was all in the hallway. I mean, we were not together for more than a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't you ask where he lived now when never returning home to his house in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He said: "I've found a flat in Prijedor." And in Omarska, he wasn't living in his own house. He was merely a tenant there. So that I didn't ask him. I knew that he was in Prijedor, and I didn't know the address. I never even asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic find this flat in Prijedor prior to the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in a position to know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Are there any questions in re-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the side of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have four or five questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher, can you please move the ELMO machine. Just back, it's in my line of vision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, what year did you get married?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned in relation to a question put to you by the presiding Judge, Judge Schomburg, you said that Dr. Stakic's brother, Baco, lived in a street with a electricity facility in Prijedor. What was the name of that electricity -- electric facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's first the electric power supply building. I mean, they have their offices there. That is the building that belonged to the company Elektricno. They were responsible for the distribution of power, but they only had -- it was only their office building. No installations were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said in a question put to you by Judge Schomburg that you knew a person nicknamed Mico whose name was Milorad Stakic, and you said that he was a relative of Dr. Stakic. How is he related to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me object to the form of the question, Your Honour. I think it mischaracterises his prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm awfully sorry, but I can't hear anything. My headphones don't work in the moment. I have to wait so I can read it. May I ask the Prosecution to break down the question in two portions; one related to Mico and then to Milorad Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, His Honour asked you about a person called Milorad Stakic, did you know of someone by that name. And you said that you knew someone who had a nickname Mico, Mico.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Baco, but Mico, Mico is somebody else, and I know him, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's correct. You said that he was a relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I at least ask that the counsel give me the page number which she is referencing to. I think by the question, although we raised it at that time in connection with the interpretation, I would like the specific page number and line number where she is making that assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As it is the rule, may I ask Ms. Sutherland to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can have a moment, Your Honour. The question that was put by Judge Schomburg was "Do you know" -- I'm sorry it's on page 15 of the LiveNote. "Do you know another member of the family of Dr. Stakic with the name of Milorad Stakic?" You answered: "There is one Mico Stakic he is a relative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I hope Defence counsel can now better understand. I already the last time said and asked the Defence counsel to refrain from frivolous objections. I'm quite sure that you followed the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to reserve my right to address the Court on that issue when the witness is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not in this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the question and answer that I just read to you. How was he related, Mico Stakic, the person that you referred to, how was he related to Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, related, I think they are quite close relatives because they have the same last name. And Doctor's father has a house nearby, but they have the same surname. And that is why I think that they are related. But what kind of a relationship there is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you're not sure whether they are blood relatives or related by marriage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the same surname. If we have the same surname, Stakic, that it could be only on the paternal side, that somehow they are related on the paternal side. But whether Milomir's father and Mico's father are -- I don't know how related they are. Are they brothers or cousins once removed, twice removed, I really cannot say. But the surname is the same, so obviously they are blood relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that for me. Again, in relation to questions by Judges Argibay and Judge Schomburg, you said that you were together with Dr. Stakic on the night of the 29th of April, 1992, the night before the takeover. This is on pages 32 and 33, at least Judge Schomburg's questioning. You went on to say that you were "with Dr. Stakic nearly every evening whenever we were off duty practically." First of all, I want to ask you about the 29th of April. You said that you didn't take Dr. Stakic home that evening, but you were together. Where were you and until what time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the yard, in mine and my brother's yard, because in his yard there were no tables, and over here there was a table. So we were sitting there in the evening from - I don't know - 7.00 or 8.00 until about 9.00. We were sitting there having a chat, having some coffee, and we were just sitting there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At that time, Dr. Stakic left your yard and returned to his?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I then went in, and he went back to his flat. And I went into my house, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you sure about the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, because what caught me by surprise that day was that we had not come together and the days that followed we did not travel together, so it stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said every evening you were together with Dr. Stakic whenever we were off duty, practically every evening. Where did you socialise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We socialised mostly in my yard and my brother's yard. We at times spent the whole on weekends playing cards or something. But by and large, it was in the yard. But naturally, if it rained then we would come into our house because there was a lot of room there. His flat was smaller. It was in the loft.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you play cards together or with others? I mean, did you only play cards with Dr. Stakic or other people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other people. Other people, too. And he, with him, sometimes three, four, five. Depends. It varied. I can't tell you how many there were when. That evening, there were my brother, he, and myself. And we did not play cards that evening. We were sitting having coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you did play cards with other people, who were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, I, my brother, the neighbour across the street, and somebody might come by because our yard is open. There's no fence there, so -- and there's a shrub in front, so somebody sees us and joins us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My question was: Who the names of the people that you played with Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragoja Rosic, my brother; Dragan Ivanovic, a neighbour. Then another neighbour, Pusac. There are three of them, and they were not always all there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're quite certain that the night before the takeover, Dr. Stakic was at your house between 7.00 and 9.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the house, in the yard. That is where we were. We were sitting there. Dr. Stakic, my brother Dragoja, and I. We were not inside. And I know that lights had gone up -- I mean, the public lighting, or rather the lighting in the yard. So we sat there for a little while longer, and then we parted company. I went in, and he went back to his flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you be mistaken about the time, 9.00?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, was it 20 to 9.00 or 9.00, I can't really say. But that is about the time when the darkness falls. That is, past 8.00, half past 8.00, it is already dark by that time so it could have been around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any further questions by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Actually I do, Your Honour, that emanate from the questions of the OTP, if I may. I would just like the Court to be patient. I would like do this as eloquently as possible with respect to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, good afternoon again. Do you recall a name of an individual in Prijedor or in Bosnia and Herzegovina by the name of Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic, yes, I've heard of Velibor Ostojic, but I don't know if he comes from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Maybe not Prijedor, but in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question to you, sir, is that this gentleman by the name of Velibor Ostojic has the exact same last name that I do. Can you tell this Court what relation that individual is to me, if any?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic, I know that he was a member of the cabinet, government of Republika Srpska. But what he was, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, sir. But surely if the gentleman by the name of Mico Stakic is somehow related because he bears the same last name as the Stakic family of Dr. Stakic, do you as you sit here that Velibor Ostojic in any way is related to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to allow this hypothetical questions not related to our case. Questions were in a line of questions related to Dr. Stakic apparently relatives as the witness has told us, and therefore, it has nothing to do with abstract names and abstract persons the witness apparently does not know. So please refrain from this line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just if I may, for the record, Your Honour. I respectfully understand the Court's position. I unfortunately disagree. The witness did recognise the name. He even gave the title that he believes that individual bears. My next question was going to be perhaps a little more abstract because there always is a basketball player that plays for Partizan that bears the same last name. It's consist with this witness's testimony, that just if you have the same last name you may be somehow related. But in any event, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, my next question to you is this: What does your wife call Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She calls him Dr. Miso.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is "Miso" his name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His name is Milomir, but she calls him Miso, my wife. And I call him Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. And now, ever since you joined the family or ever since you became married in 1974 or 1972, I think you said approximately if I may be given that latitude at least, have you ever heard anyone call Dr. Stakic by the name of Milomir, or is it, in fact, sir, that everyone who knew him at a personal level and were familiar with him called him, in fact, Miso?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, everybody called him Miso, Miso Stakic. Few people called him Milomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You described this individual called Mico who has the same last name as the family Stakic. Can you describe that individual for us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can. He's slightly older than Dr. Stakic, but he's younger than I. Of about my height. Well, he's not that stout.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I won't go there. Can you describe Dr. Stakic's brother, Baco.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baco, I can, yes. Baco is a slim guy, tall, slightly taller than I am but much slimmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you another question but I'm going to preface it because, Your Honour, with your permission I'd like to go into this area although it doesn't specifically emanate from the OTP's questions. And, Mr. Rosic, just be patient I just don't know if there's going to be an intervention, so before you answer the question. Sir, I'd like to know on how many occasions prior to this week did you have an opportunity to meet with the Defence team of Dr. Milomir Stakic, on how many occasions, if I'm allowed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try to restate the question. My apologies to you. You testified previously that the first time you were contacted from representatives of the Defence team was approximately a year or so, if I recall it properly. Within that given year, can you tell us the number of times that you met with different representatives of the Defence team of Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once as far as I know, and now, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And tell us with whom did you meet? Was it with Mr. Lukic, to speed things up, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, at that time, did you take notes or record the conversation that you and Mr. Lukic had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN ROSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't take any notes. No, nothing. We talked, I accepted to come. "Would you like to come and testify?" That was that. I didn't take any notes. I didn't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no other request for further questions. So thank you for coming to The Hague. Thank you for answering the questions. And you are excused for today. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the break, I learned that there were some issues I think from the side of the Defence to be discussed, but please briefly that we can continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I could cover them all briefly, Your Honour, quite candidly. I'll do the best that I can. I have approximately four issues I would like to address with the Court, and perhaps I will do it in reverse order because of the time. The Court asked this Mr. Rosic, the witness that just testified, for his personal telephone number. We would ask, if possible, that that be redacted from the record so that it doesn't get publicised. I'm not sure -- the Court has it and for your purposes, for whatever which they may be, the Court is welcome to it. We just wouldn't like to open up an opportunity where there is any solicitation of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No discussion with this, the telephone number would be redacted from the transcript, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I also have a request with respect to the next witness. We have about six documents that are both in Cyrillic and Latin characters that we will be presenting through the witness. The translation of those documents are not complete. We have tendered them to the Madam Registrar, and we are just waiting to get them. However, counsel for the OTP and I have spoken this afternoon in connection with this witness. It doesn't look that we can conclude him today. However, he is unavailable to proceed on Monday. He informed me of this only early this morning. The Court obviously is welcome to ask this witness that. So we're kind of in a bit after dilemma. The Defence would like the right to continue to go through some of the articles, since we are still gathering evidence, with this witness. If the witness does commence his testimony, we are obviously restricted by -- appropriately so by the guidelines set forth by the Court. So we're at a bit of a dilemma on that issue. If I may proceed to the next issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think as to the fact that you mentioned this, there would be maybe a limited time only for this witness. We can postpone the translation and the question of admission into evidence, and based on the fact that one of the Judges understand and can follow that what is shown on the Kozarski Vjesnik articles, I think it's time that we immediately start and let the discussions and other issues open for Monday. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There's two other critical issues, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: With a link to the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let us wait. We have a long waiting list of persons wanting to take the floor in this case on several issues, and I ruled that this has to wait until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Your Honour, this witness cannot be here on Monday, and that's what I'm advising the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I fully understand. But therefore, we shouldn't waste time. May I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. So in practical terms, it would mean to introduce these articles separately, maybe on Monday, with the assistance of a person able to read out these documents as we did it previously when we needed two translations, and refrain from asking questions based on these concrete articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just to the record is noted. We do object to that, and I think we have a right to ask on these articles this witness. He can read them but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is only not to read out the documents. I think you have understood. Good afternoon, and sorry that you had to wait such a long period of time. Can you hear in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind and give us your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Before we start the examination-in-chief, may I ask you, I learned that you would have some time problems, especially on Monday. Could you please explain the reason why you would not be available if so on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first reason is that I have a wedding in the family on Saturday at 1400 hours. The second reason is that I am the owner of a private company, and I have ten employees. I have postponed all of my meetings and everything else for Monday.
