So I have urgent issues to deal with for my company. I was told that my testimony would be over before Saturday. That's why I have arranged my timetable in accordance with that. And I have arranged all of my business obligations in accordance with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I think we should start immediately and try to have a fair split of the remaining time. What is your time estimate, if you can try to speed up as far as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll try my best to speed up. We estimated that it would take two hours. We think that it will take longer with the articles. Again, understanding the Court's ruling, we won't go into those articles at this time, but we think they are significant and we think they are rather relevant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll try to do the best we can. If the Court wants, this witness in his proffer sets forth specifically the items that we're going to cover with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are aware of this. And may I ask you, please, to start. And aim at concluding maybe after 90 minutes or so. Let's at least try that the witness has not to come back once again to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Mr. Plemic, can you just state your name for the record. I'm not sure your name is reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Plemic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plemic, good afternoon. My name is John Ostojic, along with Danilo Cirkovic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic. Briefly, sir, can you give us your personal background, date of birth, marital status, and place of current residence.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I was born on 18 September 1958 in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And currently --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in economics. I am married. I have two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you said adult children. Correct? Two adult daughters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The translator didn't hear it, apparently. I would just ask that you keep your voice -- or try to answer the question a little louder so that everyone can have a complete understanding of that what you're about to testify to. Sir, where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I currently reside in Prijedor. That is my official residence. But I commute between Prijedor and Belgrade because I have one company in Belgrade and one in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the spring and summer of 1992, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: In Prijedor. Up to the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us briefly what your employment history is immediately following the completion of your education. Just take us in a very brief and succinct manner the time period and exactly where you worked.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1983 in Belgrade. In 1984, I started working in the Ljubija iron ore mines, and I was the head of sales there. I stayed there until 1989. To be more precise, until August 1989. That is when I opened my own company. I started my own business. The company's name is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Santurskomerc. Its main activity is services in the field of tourism, which means the organisation of holidays, winter breaks, travels. In 1990, I opened a company Lvor in Ukraine. The name is -- it was a joint venture with a citizen of Ukraine. Up to 1991, the main business activity of my company was the organisation of travel for students and pupils, as well as the organisation of boat trips by rivers in Ukraine and Russia, the Volga and the Dniepr Rivers. I also organised students' final-year trips in many cities of Russia, Kiev, Moscow, St. Petersburg. After the year 1991, for the reasons well-known to everybody, including yourselves, my main activity was transport because my last cruising group was in September 1991. That was the last cruise I organised. I don't know whether you would be interested in anything else, but it would be mostly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll put a question to you. Subsequent or following September of 1991, can you tell us in what occupation you were in and what exactly you did as a private entrepreneur in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: In 1991, one could already feel that there was a need for the organisation of travel. People started asking for tickets. They wanted to travel abroad. They also wanted to travel domestically, and we were amongst the first in Prijedor to open a direct bus line to Zagreb. As far as I can remember, but I can't give you the exact date, this may have been the end of August 1991. After that, we established contacts with different haulers. One of them was Bosnalivno, a Livno-based company. And we were their ticketing agents for the area of the town of Prijedor. They had daily departures of their regular bus line to Switzerland and Germany. I sent my employees for a course in the JAT education centre in Belgrade. JAT was a Yugoslav air carrier. We were then authorised to sell their tickets as well. That will be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the period following September of 1991, am I correct that you were essentially a travel agent that acted as an intermediary to facilitate the purchase of tickets from your clientele who desired to buy a ticket to reach a different destination. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Partly. We sold bus tickets to Zagreb for our own bus. My agency at that time had one bus, one coach, which up to that time had mostly served to transport tourists from Zagreb to Budapest. The tourists who then proceeded to go on various cruises. The majority of my passengers at the time were booked through the company called Astratours, a Zagreb-based company. As for the tickets that we sold as mediators, we were the agents for Bosna from Livno. We got commissions for those tickets. Our passengers did not have to go to Livno to purchase those tickets. They could do it in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the time period following September 1991, could you cite for me to the best of your recollection some of your other competitors.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Well, if you mean the sale of tickets, every travel agent sold bus tickets. So that was very simple. It was simpler to sell bus tickets than air tickets because for air tickets you needed an authorisation, a license. In Prijedor, more specifically, the travel agency which had a longer history than my agency which started doing business with Bosnalivno before my agency was Olympic Tours. Among more significant agencies, there was also the agency called Autotransport Prijedor. That was the agency which was a part of the Autotransport transport company from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to Olympics transport that you mentioned, can you tell us during that time period what the name of the director was of that agency?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Emsud Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what his ethnic background is.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Probably a Muslim or a Bosniak, whichever way you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And your ethnic background, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did this Olympus -- what's the name of the company again? Help me.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: It is a company that operated as a part of the ZTP Sarajevo, ZTP stands for the railway of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was their official agency that sold tickets for rail transport. They also sold bus tickets. As far as I can remember, they also sold air tickets, but I am not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This company, did it also sell the bus tickets, railway tickets, and airline tickets the same period that you did, I mean following September 1991 all the way the spring and summer 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Since they existed, they must have been selling them. I don't know exactly what they did. They were open. They kept their business. What their business was, I can't tell you exactly. I don't know even know whether they did any business or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, sir, in the spring -- at any time in September of 1991, were you approached by any representatives from the municipal government or the Municipal Assembly who instructed you to form such a company and to start selling tickets to people who wanted to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I already gave this question. I was independent when I opened my business. Nobody ever tried to influence my business in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But for our purposes, it may be significant, and I apologise for having to ask you that. Did any political party at any time in 1991 instruct, order, or request from you that you open a company and start transporting people who wanted to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you at that time a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you at any time up to the present a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, at any time if you held any political affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: At any time. Up to 1989, I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And after that, sir, were you -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: After that, in 1990, I became a member of the party of private initiative which rallied around the self-business people, people who were mostly in business.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was the president of the party of private initiative at the time in which you were a member, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the last name is Murselovic. I can't remember his first name. We all called him Mursel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long have you known this individual called Mr. Murselovic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: A long time. A long time. That means that I knew him at least from 1977. Maybe even before that because this gentleman ran a restaurant. He had a restaurant, a restaurant that I frequently went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you also, sir, know Mr. Murselovic's wife?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was a waitress in that same restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: From September of 1991 and through the spring and summer of 1992, at the time, did you have an opportunity to employ other people in your private company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I don't know which are the first, which are the second. I can only say that there were many ethnic backgrounds amongst the people who worked for me. I can't even remember at this point in time. But this really is not important. My answer is yes, there were people of other ethnic backgrounds. But let me tell you that this was not a requirement or a condition for employment in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time discharge, terminate, or fire any employees who were of a different ethnic background than yourself who were previously employed in your company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: The only reason for firing somebody in my company was the following: If somebody fails to meet their obligations, if somebody doesn't deliver what they are supposed to. And nobody was ever fired for being of a different ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone, sir, in the municipal government of Prijedor at any time request, demand, or order you to fire individuals in your private company who were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone, sir, from the party SDS request, demand, or order you to fire, discharge, or terminate the employment of any employees who were non-Serbs from your company?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did at any time, and the time period we're focussing on again, is from September 1991 throughout the spring and summer of 1992, did at any time the municipal civilian organs of the municipality of Prijedor have any influence over you or your company as to which people could purchase tickets and which people can travel to other destinations?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: To begin with, I don't remember that I've ever had any contacts with the institutions you have referred to. And that would also imply the answer to your question. No one ever influenced in any way the work of my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Describe for us, if you will, to the best of your recollection and based upon your personal experience and observations, how is it that the people came to you after September 1991 seeking tickets to leave the area? Where were your headquarters? How many people would come by? What was the price of the ticket, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I'm allowed to ask a compound question like that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of my agency was at the Prijedor Hotel in Prijedor. A branch office was at the Balkan Hotel in the centre of Prijedor town. As concerns the modality, how people bought their tickets, we did the same as all travel agencies throughout the world. You go to an agency, you inquire whether there are any tickets available for a particular destination, and if so, if we are able to meet the client's demands, we sell the ticket according to the official price list, regardless of the fact whether it's a ticket from Bosnalivno, for which we had official prices. Regardless of the fact if it was an air ticket for which also there were fixed prices, or a ticket for Zagreb which also had a fixed official price. I'm not sure you want me to start enumerating specific prices related to specific destinations. I think I could probably remember a couple of specific prices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that might be helpful. But at this time, if you don't mind, I'd like to ask you a specific question. If you could just tell us to the best of your recollection what the route was, meaning the destination, that your company Santurs was offering during that time period for the citizens and residents of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: First of all, there was a interim exceptional line taking people to Zagreb on a daily basis. It would leave Prijedor in the early morning hours. I can't remember the exact time of departure. It was, I think, around 5.00, 6.00, or even 7.00 in the morning. And the same bus would leave Zagreb at 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon, I think. As I already said, we also sold tickets for Bosna Livno. They had regular bus lines to Switzerland, Germany, and Austria. There were air tickets, too. Departures could have been from Banja Luka, Belgrade, or Zagreb, I can't remember specifically because the agency had authorisation to sell tickets from those particular airports -- with departures from those particular airports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically with respect to your company, did you -- I think you mentioned you had a bus that the company owned, and you started selling tickets for that bus, correct, in the -- September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just explain that route to us if you don't mind. Was it daily? Several times a week? And the destination of that route?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: As concerns our own transport, there was a daily line Prijedor/Zagreb, Zagreb/Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies. Were those tickets that the people were given to travel on your bus line, sir, purchased by the municipal government of Prijedor at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell this Court how those individuals purchased those tickets since you were the ticket agent that sold them the ticket and transported them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask Defence counsel to concentrate on the fourth amended indictment and to the areas purportedly being the destination of people leaving Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think all the questions quite frankly, Your Honour, are strictly confined to that based on your prior comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't in the presence of the witness discuss certain areas mentioned in the fourth amended indictment. I would like you to concentrate on these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My focus, so the Court knows, is specifically paragraph 8 of the fourth amended indictment which addresses, I think as I've elaborated earlier. But I'm not sure -- unless the Court wants to give me the paragraph, I'll be happy to move on. But we're covering those areas as indicated in our proffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, sir, help me with this: You were the person among other individuals in your company who sold tickets to people who were leaving the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And there were other companies that were selling tickets also for people who wanted to leave the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I've said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just trying to get to where we need to go. Can you tell me, sir, with any specificity whether the people that left the Prijedor Municipality, whether they left voluntarily or involuntarily?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the concept "involuntarily."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did anyone, to the best of your knowledge, sir, forcibly transport or deport any of the individuals that you transported, that you provided a mode of transportation for, out of Prijedor during the time period that you had your agency and during the time period specifically outlined in the fourth amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: This question, I will try to be very succinct and very clear, too. Because I think this question refers to everything, ticket sales for all the other destinations, too. This means that people who wanted to travel through the assistance of my agency would simply come to my agency. They would inquire about destinations that we were able to get them to. And whenever they saw fit, they purchased tickets and left for their chosen destinations. What this means is that no one at any time was forced to go to my agency. No one was at any time forced by anyone else to go to my agency and purchase a ticket. Purchasing tickets from my agency was exclusively on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what was the ethnic background were of the individuals that you provided the mode of transportation through your company.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: My clients -- among my clients there were members of all three ethnic groups. Again, I must say that before a ticket was purchased, and as the ticket was being purchased to a person, I never asked for the person's name unless it was really necessary. Because, for example, whenever persons travelled abroad or by plane, I needed their names, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We need a break, but before we have a break, may I ask Dr. Stakic, do you feel well in the moment or do you have any problems?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a slight headache, and my head is swooning slightly. I think I could use a break, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then before the break, I have to ask you, on page 46, line 7 of today's transcript, you mentioned the reasons for not being available on Monday. The first reason you told us is that you have a wedding in the family on Saturday at 1400 hours. May I ask who are those persons having the honour to have marriage tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my brother.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the brother of my uncle who lives in Belgrade, my cousin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Based on the comments given by the witness, I expect submissions by both parties as to the question whether or not the reasons given by the witness are sufficient for excusing him from being present on Monday. The trial stays adjourned until 5:15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May I first of all ask Dr. Stakic, do you feel better now that you can follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I've managed to refresh myself a little bit. I had a cup of coffee, and I think I can make it to the end of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I hear the brief submissions by the parties related to the question whether or not the apologies to be found on page 46 of the transcript are sufficient. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence does submit that we think the reasons stated by the witness are sufficient, and I would just like to remind the Court if at all possible, although we do not have the transcript and the specific page, but to recall the testimony of Mr. Mevludin Sejmenovic who, for economic reasons which the OTP cited, was given specifically a leave of two weeks for interruption of his evidence on direct and then leave for his cross. Similarly, I think other witnesses were also provided and extended the same courtesy. And in that vein, we would respectfully request, although unbeknownst to us until this morning literally with respect to this witness, that the same courtesies be extended to him. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's two issues here, whether the Prosecution would make a submission to postpone his cross-examination due to the proffer being given to us, the amended proffer being provided at approximately quarter to 12.00 this morning which raised one new issue in paragraph (q). Secondly, it's the eight documents that we don't have translations for which were provided this morning. The Prosecution submits that the Defence could have these documents read into the transcript, but we would then require some time to cross-examine then because we would only know what the documents were about as the witness was stating the contents thereof. The second [sic] point is whether he should come back on Monday. The Prosecution submits we don't want to unnecessarily inconvenience witnesses, and that the court process should take priority over most other kinds of obligations and duties and that there normally would have to be a balance struck. Normally the parties reach agreement. And as my learned friend has just informed the Court, there was a Prosecution witness where that was done. But I leave it for the Court to decide whether the reasons given, i.e., the witness had postponed certain meetings until Monday and has some urgent issues to attend to decide whether, in fact, he should come back on Monday or to be cross-examined at a later date. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in principle, the Prosecution would be prepared to cross-examine this witness at a later date. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, depending what the witness says in relation to what's stated in paragraph (q) of the amended proffer, we may seek to postpone the cross-examination. And it's also in relation to the untranslated documents which were served on us at 1.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will decide as soon as possible and practical. But let us continue. May I ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the witness comes, although he's bringing him in, I would just like to submit to the Court that these were articles that were given to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We shouldn't discuss the articles right now. We know about the contents, and we want to hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As he's bringing him in, if I can just say, they were provided to us by the OTP. So they are not new to them. They have had them. They didn't translate it. But that's fine, we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, they were provided to the Defence upon the Defence's review of all the Kozarski Vjesnik articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are well aware of this fact. Before we start, may I ask the witness: Do you want to add anything related to the question of your return to former Yugoslavia during the weekend? Would it be possible for you to come back on Monday in principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, I would not be able to come back on Monday. Middle or the end of next week would be fine. On Monday, I have three appointments scheduled with people who are not from Belgrade or from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We will decide on this issue as soon as practicable. But please proceed, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plemic, if we may continue, help me with the appreciation and understanding of exactly the time period because there might be some confusion. From September 1991 up through and including the end of May 1992, you continued to provide transportation for people who wanted to voluntarily leave the Prijedor Municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you sold them tickets, and you also knew the place where they were going to ultimately go to. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in addition to your company, there were other companies that you previously mentioned who provided the same services as your travel agency. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me with this: During that time period as outlined in the fourth amended indictment, and I recognise you don't have that, but for our purposes, can you tell me during that time period, September 1991 through late May 1992, whether or not the police -- whether or not the police instructed, influenced, ordered, or requested that you, as a private entrepreneur with your travel business, that you provide transportation to Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats out of the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, no one interfered with the work of my agency. And I can state this with full responsibility. I don't know of a single case where someone ordered me to provide transport for anyone else. I never got any such orders from the army or from the police. After all, they were not really relevant factors for my business at that time, the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the people who were leaving the Prijedor Municipality, sir, at any time during this same time period as outlined in the indictment, did they, sir, at any time advise or inform you that the reason they were leaving the Prijedor Municipality was because of propaganda that was inciting and referring to the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats as fanatics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I kindly ask Defence counsel not to make reference to the indictment not available for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I was just doing it for the Court and the OTP. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question and refer to the concrete period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the entire period of time, Mr. Plemic, from September 1991 through the end of May 1992, did at any time any of those individuals who sought to voluntarily leave the Prijedor Municipality, did they at any time tell you that the reason they were leaving because there was some sort of propaganda referring to the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats as being fanatics?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I will try to be as concise as possible. The reasons why those people travelled, I will try to explain them in as concise a manner as I can and to the best of my knowledge. The only time that I knew personally about someone's reasons for travelling, it happened in September 1991 when some friends of mine, a group which included both Serbs and Muslims, wanted to avoid their regular military service. It was a very small number of passengers. After that, in October, November, or December 1991, people travelled as usual. There weren't very high tensions. I had no reason to ponder why those people were travelling, why they were leaving Prijedor. The only thing I did notice during that period was that the bus which returned from Zagreb contained mostly Serbs who were leaving Croatia. But none of them told me that anyone had forced them to leave. They, too, were leaving voluntarily their places of residence. None of those people ever told me that they had been under any pressure to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, did you at any time during the time period of end -- or September 1991 through the end of May 1992, did you, sir, hear or learn, observe, or personally experience during the interactions that you had with the individuals and the citizens of the Prijedor Municipality that they were involuntarily leaving the municipality or that there was some sort of preconceived plan which required that there be a forcible transfer or deportation of Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No. There were no such cases. When you are referring to the period that you mentioned, there wasn't a single such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn to another issue, if I may, Mr. Plemic. Are you familiar with - I'm just going to lead here with the permission of the Court and the OTP - did you ever hear of a plane, a Croatian plane by the name of Kikas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: The plain, the plain is the wrong word. Kikas was an aircraft plane, a passenger aircraft which the Yugoslav People's Army troops seized in Croatia and which was loaded with weapons. It was in all the information programmes on television. That plane had been seized by the army and turned over for management to the Yugoslav airline, that is JAT, because they were the only ones who had pilots trained for that particular aircraft and the servicing facilities for that aircraft. That is how that plane gained notoriety. That is what I can tell you. That is what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can find out any more about it. Did you, sir, at any time sell any tickets for this plane called Kikas?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No, no, there were no seats on that plane, and the tickets that we sell -- now I won't go into the manner how one sells tickets. There is a so-called central booking service in Belgrade, and they will approve or not every seat that we could sell or not sell. And I sold only JAT tickets for which we had license with seats with numbers and indicated names. And the fares had been set by the Yugoslav airlines. We, of course, had a commission which was usual for those who intermediated when selling tickets. Now how much it was, I don't remember. And I say with full responsibility that never, at any moment, a single employee of mine ever sold a single ticket for the plane that you mentioned or was engaged in any transport in relation to that plane. And I don't know what else you wanted to ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll get to it, thank you. My question next to you, sir, is that plane, were you able to observe that plane and the passengers that were boarding that plane in the Banja Luka airport when you were there after May 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene. I can't see the relevance of the line of these questions. May I direct then Defence counsel, please, to cover the period of time of the fourth amended indictment and to the accusations in this indictment, that is the period following the 30th of April through September 1992. And especially related to transports of persons by Autotransport Prijedor. I think it's not helpful to discuss in general one single aircraft opposed to all these buses the witnesses before had told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respectfully, Your Honour, if the Court looks at the testimony of the witness that testified in open court on page 6.771, the Court perhaps will -- at least I'll make my record that this witness has reliable and credible information that goes specifically to the credibility of that witness. But if the Court is not willing - and that's your decision - to hear the testimony, that witness specifically identified that aircraft, there was specific conclusions made by that witness in connection with the aircraft. And I think that it's necessary to have a complete appreciation that we address those issues. I will move on, and we are talking about the period within the indictment, specifically since this individual worked all the way through May 30th, so that covers the 30 days before and it covers more than just counts 6, 7, and 8 of the indictment; it specifically covers count 1, as well as count 2. But if I may, I'll proceed in accordance with the Court's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plemic, let me just try because of the necessity of time and I appreciate your patience on this, and I apologise for having to have you present during the exchange and dialogue with the Court. With respect to the period after May 30th, 1992, can you tell us what, if anything, you did professionally.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Well, even after the 30th of May, when I was in Belgrade, I had the same travel agency, that is, I was still involved in tourism, or rather, in transportation, covering the Belgrade/Budapest itinerary and also I leased buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time after May 30th, 1992, up until September 30th, 1992, provide any transportation, meaning on a intermediary basis, someone else would bring the individuals to the Belgrade area and then you would transport them to another destination as requested by your clientele, did you provide that service to people from the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me if this has to do with Belgrade, I really cannot tell you where the passengers came from because as somebody who was telling tickets, I didn't have to know that. I didn't know where somebody came from. All I needed to know was the name. That is, one didn't have to submit one's IDs to buy tickets. So who are the passengers from Belgrade, I really don't know, what was the structure there, because I wasn't directly involved in the sale of those tickets nor did I drive those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, from the period of time that you did provide transportation to citizens in the Prijedor Municipality, were your bus lines and tickets that you sold in full capacity?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: If you are asking me and as far as I could understand your question, that you were asking me about passengers from Prijedor, if that is what you're asking me, you'd also have to indicate for what period of time you are referring to. Because there were periods of time when I directly transported passengers from Prijedor to Zagreb, Austria, Germany, by bus. And there were also periods of time when I could not organise the services in that manner so that in my buses, I would take passengers who had flown in from Banja Luka, accommodate them in the buses, put them on the buses, and take them to whatever destinations they required. One bus went to Austria and another one to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us what that time period was.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I am talking about April 1992. Now, ask me what you want to know. The period that I'm talking about when I was going to Germany by bus from Prijedor, that was January, February, March, possibly April, also 1992. I'm talking when I organised the transport as such, that is not when I was merely selling tickets for somebody else. But those were extraordinary trips to Austria and Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand with your permission, I'd like to just show the witness one exhibit with the limited time just so that he could identify that that's his company because it appears in other exhibits. So since the witness is here, I would just like to lay a proper foundation in accordance with the rules that he identify - and it's a very, very short submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What would be the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 29, if the usher would be kind enough -- Defence exhibit 65 ter number 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I in the meantime ask the witness: Why do you make the distinction especially stating that this was the case January, February, March, possibly April. What happened then when you excluded, for example, May? What changed, happened in Prijedor? I make reference to page 68, line 10 of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think it is easy to explain. The bus transportation is road transportation. Now, in the middle of that particular road, there was an obstacle so that the buses could not get around it, and that is the so-called corridor. So that it was impossible to use buses as there were combat operations there and it was too dangerous for passengers, and as a travel agency we did not want to assume the responsibility for the lives of those passengers. And I believe it was around Brcko -- that was the name of the town. No, I think it was Brcko. That corridor was closed. And also the corridor leading to Croatia was also closed so that the only way was if we wanted to organise transportation by bus. Now, I'm referring to April and May. I'm certain about May. I'm not sure about April, but I'm quite positive about May. In other words, it was technically impossible. It had nothing to do with the state of affairs in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this later on. And may the Defence proceed, please, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Plemic, you're looking at the ELMO, Defence Exhibit Number 65 ter number 29. Can you just identify for the Court the publication in which this exhibit is and the date on which it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would ask the booth if they can just zoom in on the top left-hand corner, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: 27th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, sir, do you see an advertisement that is being provided in this --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whose advertisement is it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: My agency's.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the right of that, sir, there's certain indications and certain material that's on this publication. Can you just quickly by gleaning to the left of your publication, can you just tell us generally what is it that is being published in this Kozarski Vjesnik on the date that you provided us in 1991? What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: If you mean other advertisements, I can read it to you. Velika Gorica Prijedor, I'm changing and selling a flat. Velika Gorica is in Croatia. These are advertisements, and these advertisements include some of the services that I offered. And I already told you that there were regular lines to Germany, Switzerland, and Austria. And I was in this way subcontractor. There was an extraordinary line leaving to Zagreb, leaving at 6.00 in front of the office in the Balkan Hotel, that was my bus, and then below it says airline tickets for the JAT Airways. Do you want to continue reading advertisements?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In light of the time, Mr. Plemic. No, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the Defence at this time does not have any more questions of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a short 15-minute break before I start cross-examination -- or 10-minute break if we start back at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It also gives us time to have the necessary deliberations. So the trial stays adjourned until 6.00 sharp. --- Break taken at 5.52 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just apologise for keeping you for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, first of all, the Prosecution -- sorry, the Defence, it was on purpose that the Defence did not cover additional areas mentioned in the amended proffer we received only this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In part, Your Honour, but it was also the Court's constraints on the time parametres that were outlined for us. So we also wanted to give adequate time for the OTP to conduct their cross-examination so that the witness can be excused today, so in part it was, and in part it was based on the Court's instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So from your point of view, you can't see any prejudice for your client due to the time limitations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, that's unfortunately, Your Honour, not for me to conclude. So no, I cannot conclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to state that you, in fact, did not exhaust the time given to you in total, and this should be reflected on the transcript. So therefore, it would have been for you and it would be for you to cover another area if you so want. I want to avoid in the interest of the witness that later on, the one or the other party submits that he would have needed this witness for additional purposes to cover additional areas. We went through the entire portions, and I think it was on purpose that, for example, you didn't cover the area under (q).

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. But I thought I tried, and the Court intervened and prohibited me from inquiring about the areas involved in (q). And I cited the specific page number of the transcript that I was going to deal with, 6.770 and 6.771. I truly cannot do any more than be that specific. And I spent approximately an hour -- to my estimation, an hour and five minutes. I wanted to extend the same courtesy to my learned friend of the OTP, and that is why I ceased, among other reasons as stated, the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So based on these remarks, let's proceed with the cross-examination. Maybe you can limited yourself in the same way. If not, let us please know. Then we would have to decide how to proceed, whether or not the witness would have to come back or to stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm just a little confused at the moment because on the discussion that I had with my learned friend from the break, it was -- and he can correct me if I misstate. His intention was to admit -- seek to tender all of these documents. If they are admitted, I would like to have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness on them. But of course, I can't today because I don't know the contents because I haven't been able to sit down with a language assistant because I have been on my feet all afternoon and since they were provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we can all agree that these documents can't be translated today, nor can they be read out by the witness. So in any event, this area can't be covered. And if there should be additional important and relevant questions, then it might be that we would have to ask the witness to come another time to The Hague. So please continue based on the area covered by the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Plemic, isn't it true that there was a lot of Serb propaganda on both the television and the radio prior to May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Are you waiting for my answer? You have finished with your question, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain, then, what kind of propaganda do you have in mind? What is your question about? You asked me whether there was any Serbian propaganda on television by Serbs? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Instilling fear in the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You don't recall seeing any propaganda at all by the Serbs on television or hearing any propaganda on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I would just like to say that I am not one of those people who watched television much. I use all my time -- at that time, that is, I used all my time to engage in my business. Most of the time I was away on business. And to be honest, I still do not understand what do you mean when you say "Serb propaganda instilling fear." What is that supposed to be? Would that be showing some killings or things like that? What do you mean by propaganda? Can you give me an example and illustrate what such kind of propaganda would look like, and then I may be able to tell you whether I heard or saw something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Killings, racial slurs.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: I never saw something like that. I claim that in full responsibility. I never saw a footage of somebody being killed on television. But again, it depends on what television you have in mind. There were different channels. You could watch programmes from Zagreb, from Belgrade, Bosnian channels as well. Let's make the long story short. I've never seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've never heard anything on television about the number, the percentage of Muslims that should be allowed to stay in the Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, what Krajina? Which Krajina? There are several Krajinas. Are you referring to Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Krajina in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO PLEMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I've never heard anything like that on either television or radio, nor have I read anything like that anywhere. I did listen to the radio, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This gives, no doubt, the possibility for the Defence to add those questions not covered during the examination-in-chief, and hereby I reopen the examination-in-chief for the Defence. Your witness, Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm put in a very difficult position. And I'm not sure -- in any event. We're going to tender to the witness the following exhibits for purposes of identification under the Defence 65 ter number as previously submitted to the Madam Registrar and I believe to the Court, and disseminated to the OTP. Exhibit 65 ter number Defence 11, 29, 78, 79, and 81. We're asking the Court to admit those documents in evidence. In light of the witness's very own testimony on the bases that he set forth, the Defence does not at this time have any questions of this witness and will reserve its right and will make the necessary and appropriate application in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, you have tendered document 65 ter number Defence 29. This will be provisionally marked D71B. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Because we don't know what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be admitted in those parts read out by the witness only. Admitted in those parts read out by the witness as D71B. And then may I ask the Defence to use the time the witness is here in order as previously said, we want to avoid that this witness has to come once again. A number of areas have not yet been covered, so please it's your time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. But help me understand this, if I may. The Defence is prepared to stay here all night to finish this witness. This Court has instructed if we ask about these exhibits, the OTP has insisted they wanted additional time to inquire on these exhibits. If they are completed with their evidence, we will attempt even though the OTP gave us the Kozarski Vjesnik, because it was in their possession after they subpoenaed and took those documents, for them to claim that as an issue we will deal with later. At this time, we do not have any further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's your submission that the only remaining questions would be based on these articles of Kozarski Vjesnik given to us under Exhibit Numbers 11, 34, 78, 79, 81, and then another article on the previous admitted document S4. But I think it's possible to base a number of questions as you wanted and as your proffer shows not linked to these articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Just so that the record is clear, the articles are not just from Kozarski Vjesnik, there's one from Oslobodenje -- or two articles from Oslobodenje just so that the Court is clear on that, and those are articles that other witnesses will hopefully -- will try to tie up. I will not proceed with the direct examination based on the constraints. The Court set the equal time for the parties with respect to this witness. The OTP has chose to waive their right to cross-examine. We think we have enough. We're not going to reopen the case so that the OTP can revisit their questions and put new questions to the witness. I respectfully would submit that if the Court deems these documents to be relevant, which we do, that the Court ask the witness questions revolving around counts specifically 1 and 2 of the fourth amended indictment, as well as counts 7 and 8 of the fourth amended indictment. Population and census is a very important factor in this case. The OTP was given an opportunity to have a demographer to testify about that. The Defence was denied that right. We're attempting to show through documentary evidence the accurate status of the population and the demographics as they existed in the Prijedor Municipality in 1992. With all due respect, the Court also gave the OTP the rights to have individuals who purport to be with the International Red Cross testify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please stop to abuse the time for these arguments. I asked you to please to proceed with the examination-in-chief, those areas as you previously mentioned that might cause prejudice to your client.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. If I may interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd rather that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't mean to be difficult, Your Honour, but the Defence has just sought to tender the remainder of the articles. I'm making an application now to put off cross-examination of this witness on any of these articles if they are going into evidence because I can see for the very short time that I've had to look at them, there's handwriting scribbled on some of these documents in numbers. For example, on 81, there's a number of handwritten numbers on what looks like ads to me, but I don't know. I respectfully request that further questions can be asked of this witness by the Prosecution and that he not be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I represent the defendant, number one. But number two, Your Honour, I invite them to see from the original documents that they gave us those are the same numbers that appear. Also, which is why I choose to tender to this witness specifically Defence exhibit under 65 ter number 29 so that he can identify his company. That company, in my opinion, is plainly revealed on this document with the date which we think is significant, and that is the area that we were going to question him on. I think it's self-evident. I think the Court since they marked most of the documents provisionally -- I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I correct you. Until now, none of the documents is marked provisionally. They are -- only one is admitted into evidence. I asked you please to proceed with questions not linked to these documents because apparently, you had these documents in your possession. We asked you several times during the last months whether you had the necessary translation. And I can understand the other party that they first want to go into details of these documents. And so therefore, please proceed with those questions having no link to these documents. And please understand that the Judges already have examined these documents and we know what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that. Your Honour, all the testimony that I -- and all the questions I would ask this witness are directly linked to these documents. And therefore based on the Court's ruling, we do not have any more questions, and respectfully would advise the Court of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no further questions from the Bench. I take it that there are no further questions with the caveat we from the Defence. There are no other questions from the side of the Prosecution for the reasons everybody can read in the transcript. And therefore, we have to conclude your testimony. We have to apologise that you had to stay such a long period of time due to reasons you are not responsible for. And you are excused for today, but unfortunately, you have followed the discussion, it might be necessary to invite you another time to come back to The Hague. But in the limited time, about 30 minutes, it wouldn't be possible adequately to cover these documents, first of all, because they are not translated in a language that is not an official language of this Tribunal. And secondly, unfortunately, against our rules, the Defence provided the Trial Chamber with a proffer - that means a preparation of your testimony - scheduled for Tuesday or Wednesday only this morning. And therefore, it might be necessary for these shortcomings by the side of the Defence to recall you once again to The Hague. I hope this will not be necessary, but I can't exclude this. So therefore, you are excused for today, and I wish you a safe trip home. I hope you will be in time back for this marriage as you told us that will take place. Thank you once again for coming to The Hague. Have a safe trip home. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's now to decide how to proceed on Monday. May I ask the Defence whether or not there is an additional witness available for Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Regretfully, Your Honour, there is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we would then have to proceed with a number of issues already announced by both parties. There was a request by the, in the moment, absent lead counsel of the Prosecution to be heard on some issues. There was a request by the Defence to be heard on some issues. We have some documents. May I ask for submissions by the parties on the question how to proceed on Monday. What has priority? It's the Defence case, so please, Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would submit, as we did during the 65 ter conference, to the extent that we could conclude the witnesses that are present at The Hague, that the Court not convene on Monday, February 10th, since apparently we've concluded with the witnesses that are here. We did yesterday, in light of the length of the prior witness and the other issues that developed this previous Monday, we called and rescheduled the witnesses who were going to arrive today for Monday, and as the Court said, possibly Wednesday although that was changed. We at this time do not believe that there are any pressing issues relating to this case that would necessitate the Court to convene on Monday respectfully. There is one issue that during the initial start of these proceedings today I asked to be heard on. We would just like to make a quick reference to it if permitted so that it's on the record, and it's an issue that was raised during the 65 ter conference. If I'm just permitted to raise it, and then the Court can decide whether or not you'd like to hear more on that issue or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm aware -- you mentioned two issues, but let's first decide what is the submission by the Prosecution related to a hearing on Monday or not. Please be aware about the costs of a precious day here in the courtroom, deplorable not used for the purposes of a hearing if we can't proceed on Monday. So may I ask, what is your submission?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we don't have any witnesses, we can't proceed apart from the hearing that the senior trial attorney has requested. I can speak with her this evening on the telephone and advise your legal officer whether she would like to be heard on Monday or whether it can be put off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then first address proprio motu another issue. As said previously, we can't continue in this way that we receive the proffer for the upcoming witness that same morning when the witness is heard in the afternoon. The witness was called. He came on Tuesday, and I'm quite sure it was possibly to have an adequate proffer ready for today earlier, and this would have avoided all these problems we are facing today. Especially it would have been possible, and I advised Defence counsel several times, whenever there is a problem with a translation, please indicate this to the Trial Chamber, and as you may recall, yesterday always there will be a way to overcome these problems. So if you would have told us that it would be absolutely necessary for the hearing of this witness, no doubt it would have been possible to translate these documents in a language we understand and which would give the other party the opportunity to follow this and maybe come to other parts of the same document. So therefore, the Defence should know that in future, we will only proceed with the consent of the other party and the consent of the Judges when we are in the possession of the necessary proffers as late as it was the case this week. The ruling was that the proffer should arrive at least - and it was already in a special advantage for the Defence - at least two days prior to the hearing in order that the other party and the Judges can prepare the hearing of this witness. So please take care that the proffers arrive in this due time. We'll say no later than two days before the witness appears. And we would only continue with the consent of the Prosecution and the Judges if these documents do not arrive in due time. Whenever you want to make use of documents in the moment only available in B/C/S and for reasons we don't know, these documents are not yet translated, please tell us also two days in advance that we take the necessary measures that these will be translated in due time. Otherwise, we would have to skip and to cancel the hearing, and this would go on the account and to the detriment of the Defence. The time is absolutely limited. You know the time limits; you know that the Secretary-General of the United Nations already has ordered the beginning of the next trial. He has already assigned the Judges for the next case to hear these cases here in The Hague is a precious good, and we shouldn't waste any time. And if a party fails to obey the rules, unfortunately it's to the detriment of this party. We discussed this already previously. I hope that the fact that we have a break next week will serve this purpose, and we will continue in a more civilised way after this break. But let's make use of the time later on to discuss the issues you wanted to raise. But I can see the representative of the Prosecution was first on her feet. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may assist the Defence if whatever exhibits they are going to use with the witnesses, if they haven't been translated, to even provide us two days before with the numbers, and then we can have a language assistant look at those actual Rule 65 ter documents and it may have alleviated -- if we were told of the numbers for today, I could have had a language assistant look at those documents and I may have had questions or I may not. But that's just one suggestion of maybe providing the numbers two days before, and we can have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this additional hint. And it may serve the interests of the Defence. So please make use of all these offers given to you. So may I hear your intervention on the two issues you mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour. If I may just respond very, very briefly on the other issue. I think it's in the transcript from yesterday, we did mention the time constraints that we were under and we did mention with respect to this specific witness the proffer was late. We do recognise the rules that have been set in this case, and we are grateful that the Court has been flexible in terms of submitting our proffers. With this particular witness, I think the transcript will reflect - if my memory serves me correct - that we would make the submission to the Court and to the OTP by 11.00 yesterday evening. We did, because I was involved in it personally, did ultimately conclude the typing of that proffer after meeting with the witness for several hours, and submitted it to the Court and to the OTP through I think Ms. Karper at approximately midnight. We recognise that and brought it to the Court's attention yesterday. That was when we received it. We did not meet with this witness beforehand, as we told the Court, because as Mr. Lukic identified other restrictions were placed on him. We accept the Court's suggestion and invitation that those items be cured. But up to this point they were an obstacle for the Defence. So we would have to sit with the witness for that extended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond. There doesn't need to be two Defence counsel in the courtroom. That's why there's co-counsel. One counsel can be out speaking with the next witness to come along. In relation to receiving the proffer at midnight last night, I specifically asked Defence to email it to myself because I knew Ms. Karper was not going to be at her computer first thing this morning. And hence, that's why I didn't get it until quarter to 12.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I can clarify that very quickly. I think Ms. Sutherland gave it to Mr. Lukic who, based on representations just shared with me, did misplace her email address. We apologise for that inconvenience. I believe Ms. Sutherland can verify she did not give me the email address. But in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There's an old Roman saying "minima non curat praetor," the Judges are not interested in those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We should discuss only general problems. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence would like to once again raise the issue that we raised in our 65 ter conference with the OTP's, in our opinion, respectfully to the Court, intimidation of the Defence witnesses. Specifically we raised during the 65 ter conference that the investigators and the OTP have contacted a witness that has previously given sworn testimony to this Court. Specifically, that witness is now being called and has been called on numerous occasions, and it is our understanding that the OTP has now made personal contact with this witness, despite the fact that the Court was rather clear on Tuesday as to how we should proceed relevant to that witness. That witness we believe gave essential elements relating to the fourth amended indictment. The OTP is going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's, please, into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's simply not true. Likewise, the OTP insists although they know because they have the personal identification numbers of all the individuals who worked at that Detention Centre, that the Milorad Stakic that is referred to that goes by the name of Mico and not Braco is a totally different and unrelated person. That individual's father has the name of Vlado. That evidence is known to the OTP. And I think that it is by virtue of their questions that they are not simply clouding the issues before this Court or making a mockery by asking lay witnesses whether or not someone with the same last name would be related or not. But quite candidly, the Defence is prepared on that issue if the OTP is likewise to be prepared to suggest that they will withdraw their indictment if there's any evidence to remotely suggest that Dr. Stakic's brother was at any time at the Omarska Detention Centre. Facts not introduced into as evidence lead us to only speculation and conjecture. It is respectfully submitted that it is a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is respectfully submitted that it is a complete waste of time to continuously raise frivolous issues that the OTP know and are aware of since they litigated the Omarska and Keraterm cases in full, are familiar with all the parties, all the members who were involved there, and have never raised either through the indictment, their pre-trial brief, or any witnesses that they have called despite the fact that there were in excess of 52, any evidence to suggest that. Why now are we permitted to raise facts not in evidence? If they have a fact to suggest that Dr. Stakic's brother was at any time at the Detention Centre, tell us who the witness is, identify when you believe that he was there, and bring the witness in. Gladly we will allow them to reopen the case. It is simply not in our view respectfully appropriate to have now the Defence go out and find this Mico, state completely his lineage with respect to whether or not there's any relation to Dr. Stakic, and also now call his brother as a witness so that he can deny bald assertions with no bases supported by any facts whatsoever. It happened on no less than three occasion. We're merely asking for guidance that since we were prohibited from asking questions without specific articles, citations of all their witnesses that they likewise, if they are going to put a question to a witness as to whether or not there's any evidence to support that, let them present it to the Defence and let them present it to the witness. There is undoubtedly no evidence whatsoever to suggest that Dr. Milomir Stakic's brother was ever in Omarska. If they believe that it was true, they would have brought forth that evidence. They truly and honestly in their heart know that the Milorad Stakic that's identified in the fuel consumption records that the Court examined, which I believe is S375, is not Dr. Milomir Stakic's brother and is not related to him in any manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the second question, my only comment is I can't see anything about Dr. Milomir Stakic's brother in the fourth amended indictment. If it would be the Prosecution's case that this Milorad Stakic mentioned in this document is or would be the brother of Dr. Stakic, then it -- the burden of proof no doubt would be for the Prosecution and it's nothing, and absolutely nothing for the Defence to reject by evidence this attempt to identify the person mentioned in the document as the brother of Dr. Stakic. Therefore, it's absolutely nothing to do for the Defence. And they shouldn't waste -- the Defence shouldn't waste the time by continuing or trying to prove that this was not the brother. The burden of proof is quite clear. And as regards the second point, it's also quite clear, and there was a ruling by this Bench that it's absolutely irrelevant what was the reason why Dr. Stakic travelled after 1992 to what area so ever, especially after the indictment, after the issue of the arrest warrant. We can't draw any inferences from this fact whatever Dr. Stakic did. So therefore, it's absolutely irrelevant, and we ruled that we will not admit any evidence on this point. I hope the next week will, in fact, help us to continue during the end of the Defence case more precisely and more accurately concentrated on the main question of this case. And this is the link, Dr. Stakic, to the alleged charges of the fourth amended indictment and to that what happened at that point in time in Prijedor. And we should, in fact, not waste our time with side issues. And this was also one aspect of our rulings of today when we heard this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just about Monday, do you want me to contact Ms. Korner and ask her about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think as to the fact that there is no witness available on Monday, we should resume only on Monday, that is -- don't let me make a mistake - the 17th of February as scheduled. You have received the just-filed revised scheduling order, and there it reads that we then would continue Monday, the 17th of February, 9.00 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure, but I don't know whether Ms. Korner is available on the 17th and 18th of February. I think she has got other obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think there are counsel enough from the Prosecution. And as you mentioned correctly to the other side, one counsel in fact is enough. So therefore, unfortunately her statement or comments have to be postponed until she is available again for the purpose of this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour, it's just that you mentioned that she had wanted to raise a matter, and therefore I was just advising when she was going to be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think for the for -- for these purposes, it is absolutely not necessary to have an entire day in Court. So therefore, we will proceed Monday, the 17th of February, 2003. And I want to alert the Defence that that is the latest day for any 92 bis motion, and especially with the necessary prerequisites to be found in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence under 92 bis(A) as we previously ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not -- just one minute, please. Quickly, if I may. The Court I thought previously ruled and our understanding was February 24th. I believe it was in the transcript as it indicated. We would just say because we are doing a number of things with the videolink, that we be given until at least mid-week. We will attempt even before that date to identify the individuals and to tell the Court and the other party the area in which they will offer this statement. Because there's 24 specific witnesses that we hope to present in 92, we won't be able to get the entirety of the 92 bis statement prepared within that one-week period. But we can give you certainly the topical area and the identification of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can't accept this. The ruling was quite clear. The deadline for the 92 bis motion is already overdue, is set for Monday, 17th of February, 2003. And we can't prolong this. It's already doubtful now whether the procedure necessary to decide whether or not it's possible to hear these witnesses under 92 bis, to assign a presiding officer, can be done in the short time limited we have to our disposal. So therefore, we can't change. Once again, as we ruled previously, the deadline is and will be the 17th of February. Let's call it a long day. And the trial stays adjourned until Monday, 17th of February, 2003, 9.00.
